subject: Regarding Abravanel Hall
comment: Hello, After graduating from BYU in 1995, my mother started singing locally here in Salt Lake City and was soon "discovered" by Maestro Maurice Abravanel who was then leading the Utah Symphony. Over the course of a 40 year world-renown career as a performer and teacher, my mother sang almost 500 performances at the Metropolitan Opera in New York City and ended her career as a beloved vocal professor at the University of Utah. Abravanel put Utah on the cultural map, and the auditorium that bears his name is one of the very best acoustic halls in the United States. Not to mention the fact that the Utah Symphony is a world-class institution, and Salt Lake City is the smallest U.S. city to have a full time symphony orchestra. The tremendous pride we take in the Utah Symphony and in Abravanel Hall seems to have been miscalculated or overlooked in the recent conversations about the new downtown entertainment district. Abravanel Hall is a cultural landmark, and the acoustical experience it provides for thousands of music fans is not something that can be easily replicated. I join many in asking the City Council to either earmark a percentage or dollar amount of money to go toward a renovation of Abravanel Hall as part of the participation agreement. Please also provide that this funding is contingent upon Salt Lake County deciding that Abravanel Hall will remain on-site within the SECC District, in its present performances hall form and location. subject: Please Save Abravanel Hall
comment: Aloha, My name is Irminsul. I am a composer, music producer and proud Utah native, now living in Hawai'i. I grew up with Abravanel Hall as an imposing and inspirational institution. Home base for the world renowned Utah Symphony and its long string of world class conductors and performers. I personally knew a lot of them. Not only did it put Utah on the orchestral music map, it was a gem that I and many aspiring home town composers and performers had our eye on: The privilege and honor it would be to play such a place as this was always in mind. The prize. I went to so many incredible concerts there, I've lost count. Even though my own music has now been on world stages, I always dreamed that one day before I die I could have it on stage at Abravanel Hall as well. When I heard of the threat to its existence, I couldn't believe it. Who would do such a thing and whatever for? A pro hockey facility? Well here we are. The arts are now under attack nationwide. Gov Ron DeSantis has basically cut its heart out in Florida, and I have many colleagues in 15 different states telling me the same drama is going on in their states. Budgets slashed or eradicated. Concert halls being shut down. Where does it stop before we completely gut the internal organs of our culture and history? Please, please do what you can to save Abravanel Hall. I do not want to be the last generation of musicians to have experienced and taken our inspiration from the sweet shimmering sounds of its halls. Sincerely, Irminsul Volcano, HI -- Irminsul on Bandcamp

Unfortunately, I am not impressed with this deal. First and foremost, requiring that the hockey and basketball teams stay at the site for only 30 years is inadequate. Any agreement worth it's weight should require the teams to be there for at least 99 years. As the current agreement is structured, the Group could simply threaten to move the teams right as taxpayers are finished paying them millions of dollars. This deal ensures continued economic blackmail of city residents and is unacceptable. Second, why are taxpayers giving money to SEG to develop anything outside the Delta Center? Does the city really believe that if the land east of the Center was opened for development, no developer would develop it without public monies? This is prime real estate at the heart of downtown, for crying out loud, and we are just expected to hand the SEG $375 million dollars. What a waste of taxpayer dollars! Third, I am disappointed that Japantown is an afterthought in this plan, regulated to a small space within the district. The city should make the entire two blocks of the Center Japantown. The city could work with the Japanese-American community on what they would like to see in this area and set zoning and design standards to ensure the correct aesthetic. Instead, the district will be just another modernist spot filled with bars, restaurants, and housing. We are just re-creating the Gateway with taller buildings. We don't need two Gateways! An actual robust Japantown would be a great asset to the city but we are throwing that opportunity away along with millions in taxpayer money. To conclude, this plan falls far short of what is acceptable to me. I'm sure I speak for many voters in District 5 as I encourage you to vote against this raw deal for Salt Lake City taxpayers. subject: Sports and Entertainment district and Abravanel Hall
comment: Hi, I am Jack Clark, the originator of the petition to save Abravanel hall and avid supporter of the symphony. As well as someone who is not opposed to development that is within natural bounds. I am reaching out today regarding the new proposed sports and entertainment district and my opposition to the aforementioned item. First, I am not opposed to bringing the NHL team and the continual presence of the Utah Jazz in Salt Lake City. I am opposed to an extreme redevelopment of this put on the burden of the taxpayer. As well as the height of buildings that in my personal opinion the height restrictions should not be changed for a large Times Square-esque tower that will be right next to temple Square which is sacred to many and could be seen as an unfortunate juxtaposition. If not that a compromise could be achieved by not allowing the use of "jumbotrons" or screens on the buildings. Next, the tax increase is quite ironic due to the fact that we the people would be financing a billionaire's boyish dreams. He has plenty of money to redo downtown to his needs, why not allow him to use his own money. As well as that the burden of the sales tax would be put on the poor. It would cause undo burdens during shopping for the essentials such as groceries, which have increased in price significantly since the COVID-19 pandemic. This tax would also disproportionately affect the west side where the socioeconomic level is much lower than the east side. Thus causing the West side to continue the continual vicious cycle that does not allow it to prosper and puts its citizens in a very unfortunate position. To add to that, financing a new or renovated stadium on public funds is proven not to really help the economy. I recommend reading this article while I do not agree that we should not bring the NHL to Utah I am opposed to using public dollars to finance the team. https://digitalcommons.coastal.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1103&context=honors-theses The amount of money used to do this has very small returns in the grand scheme of things, and the money in Salt Lake City could be used better in other places. Finally, why should we make Salt Lake City like every other big city? Salt Lake's history is unique, its design, its architecture, and its people. We should strive to keep it that way in a manner that is sensitive to the past. Why not with his money Ryan Smith has to have a full restoration of Japan Town as a condition of his renovation if that is the will of the council. I also feel like this tax should go up for a public vote so that the public can decide if they want to bear the burden of a sports team. This would allow for the time necessary for a public discourse around this big thing. In all, I thank you for your time and consideration in reading my comments. Yet I feel we are moving too quickly and that taxes should not be imposed on the taxpayer for financing a sports team where the average person in Salt Lake City could not afford a seat. In fact, downtown needs very little "revitalization" as it is great as it is. The walkable part of our shared city. In the end I feel like this should be put up for a public vote on this tax, or the city council should shoot down this proposal in its infancy for the sake of the citizens of Salt Lake City. Regards, Mr Clark

comment: Dear City Councilmember: I urge you to oppose the proposed citywide sales tax increase that would give nearly $1 billion to the NHL sports/entertainment district. These compounding costs amount to more than $11,000 a year for the average family of four! We should not be subsidizing businesses and billionaires at the expense of the average working family. The risks that private businesses choose to take should not be placed on the backs of taxpayers, especially when that business alone stands to reap the financial rewards! Study after study shows that these subsidies do not provide the promised economic benefits, and often leave taxpayers with broken promises and mounting costs in the long run. subject: Concern re Smith group plan - D2
comment: Dear Mr. Puy, I'm a resident of Poplar Grove, and while I recognize that our neighborhood here on the West Side will likely not be directly affected by the Smith Entertainment Group plan for downtown, I am very concerned with the plan. To the extent that I have been able to learn about it, this massive project seems like it has almost carte blanche to change a very significant area in the heart of our city. I recognize that I don't have all the information, and that this plan would also bring about a lot of jobs--and, ostensibly, business once it's finished--but I'm worried about how much of downtown would be dedicated to this singular purpose. Even if we do still have other venues with purposes other than athletics within the plan (as an aside, do also consider this my plea to keep Abravanel Hall where it is) the overhaul of this crucial area for the purpose of athletics seems like a lot of upheaval for, essentially, one industry owned by one group. (Yes, I'm also aware that the LDS church owns an enormous amount of downtown, but that's not on this meeting's agenda.) On that same note, I am concerned about how much of this plan's cost would fall on taxpayers, either through city contributions or tax breaks. I am aware of the ecosystem created by a new or expanding business. I understand the arguments in favor of incentives like city contributions or tax breaks. I know that more businesses and more traffic to these venues would benefit the city in various ways. But in this case, the organization appears to overwhelmingly benefit from the arrangement, and is owned by extremely wealthy people. This feels somewhat like Donald Trump, self-aggrandized rich person, asking his much less affluent supporters for campaign contributions. One of the things that makes downtown great, and that enriches my life (a short distance away from it, is the sheer variety of businesses and events found there. The convention center draws a vast array of industries. If you come by mass transit or snag a good parking spot, you can catch a movie, see a live concert or ballet or play, lean about space, take in some art, or just have a great shopping trip--or all of the above, since they're all within an easy walk from each other. Our small, local restaurants and bars give flavor to any night out. Athletics are part of that bouquet of experiences that we boast of having downtown, but I hope the Salt Lake City Council would see the wisdom in balancing all of the individual parts for a stronger, more collaborative, and more enticing whole. Thanks for all you do for our city and for our neighborhood. Sincerely, Lisa Christensen

subject: Preserve Abravanel Hall
comment: Hello, City Council! • My name is Rosalie Lund Macmillan. I am a lifelong Utahn. My family has lived in Utah for generations. • I come from a very musical and artistic family, which is not uncommon in Utah. The arts are deeply embedded in our Utah culture and have been for generations. • The National Endowment for the Arts ranks Utah number one in the nation for live participation in the arts. • I believe the greatest catalyst for the explosive growth of the arts in Utah was the creation of Abravanel Hall. • Our relatively small community voted to raise the funds and many donated very generously so that we could build a world-class concert hall. What does that say about our community and our priorities in Utah? • It was the greatest hall in the West. People traveled from all over the country to come. It was designed by the acoustic genius who designed the famous Avery Fisher Hall in New York. I've been told it's one of the top three acoustical halls on the planet. • When you have a world-class hall, you are able to host world-class music. My family got to meet Yo-Yo Ma and help him name his cello. I got to meet Itzhak Perlman. I got to hear Jessye Norman sing in person. I had the opportunity to be mentored by the great Joseph Silverstein. Would any of this have happened if we didn't have Abravanel Hall? Absolutely not! This world-class hall attracted world-class talent which then brought even more talent and extraordinary teachers into our community. The existence of Abravanel Hall has directly affected the trajectory of my life and the lives of many others. • We didn't have to fly to New York City or the great capitals of Europe in order to be exposed to the world's greatest music and musicians. Incredibly, we got to experience that right here in our relatively much smaller hometown. • Abravanel Hall was brand new when I was a little girl. It was called Symphony Hall back then. I attended regularly with my family then, and have attended ever since. Now I attend with my young children. • Many of the strongest core memories of my life have taken place in Abravanel Hall. • I still remember the moment vividly when I was about seven years old, staring up at the beautiful chandeliers, and feeling overwhelmed by the gorgeous music I was hearing when I made the conscious decision that I wanted to be a musician when I grew up. I decided right then and there that my lifelong goal was going to be to play on that glorious stage one day. • I assure you I was not the only kid who has had that dream. There is a whole generation of us who grew up listening to world-class music in Abravanel Hall. There are hundreds of us from that first Youth Guild that was formed, so many of us checking costs in order to get extra tickets. I have kept in touch with many of them over the years. We have grown up to become music lovers, both amateurs and professionals, some nominated for Grammys, others breaking records on YouTube, and even some who play in the hall every week as members of our Utah Symphony. Collectively, our music students number in the tens of thousands. We are in turn influencing a new generation of music lovers who also have access to world-class music because of our world-class hall. • My most recent core memory in Abravanel Hall took place at one of the many concerts I have attended with my children. I looked over to see my young daughter, completely lost in the music, and gazing up at the chandeliers like I used to as a child. My young son leaned in and whispered, "Do you think I could do that someday?" motioning to the musicians onstage. I whispered back, "Absolutely." • I'd like to see my kids on that stage. I'd like to see my grandkids on that stage! • Our community made waves when they first built this hall and sent a really strong message about the priority of arts in our community. What message are you sending to our arts-loving community if you destroy it? Thank you for your consideration. Rosalie Macmillan

comment: Hello City Council, I unfortunately ran out of time and wanted to share my full comments on the Participation Agreement: Mayor Mendenhall, City Council Members and staff, Thank you for your time. My name is Marisa Eng and I am a member of the SLC NextGen JA group and Salt Lake Buddhist Temple Board. I wanted to speak today in regards to the participation agreement that was voted on earlier this evening. First, I want to thank each of you, as well as our community leaders, SEG and the public for listening and for your advocacy and commitment to preserving and revitalizing Japantown. It was very heartening to see Japantown included in the participation agreement with the $5million earmarked for revitalization efforts and for working to include us in the planning and development conversations to come. It feels like a step in the right direction. While it is a positive step forward and probably felt like somewhat of a sprint, I know this process will be a marathon and there is still a long road ahead to work out the details. After reading through the agreement, I want to acknowledge that I am still cautious and there are still several concerns that I want to ensure are considered as the process continues with you, SEG, the County, and State. As longtime neighbors and community stakeholders, it is crucial that the Salt Lake Buddhist Temple and Japanese Church of Christ are involved in the process and we welcome and encourage discussions more than twice a year as well as having ongoing dialogue and partnership post development. I also want to ensure that we preserve the temple, church and garden that is there today. The daily and annual festival operations should be able to continue without disruption from additional traffic and throughout construction. I ask that we continue to work with the county and state on parking arrangements for festivals and road accessibility for daily function and festivals. Lastly, I am hopeful that we can meaningfully honor the work and legacy of our Japanese American ancestors. Let's continue what was started with the RDA streetscape to reimagine and develop Japantown to be a space that welcomes and celebrates the diversity, culture, and history of Japantown. Along with the streetscape, having Japanese or minority-owned small businesses or spaces on the street can help cultivate that vision and activate a cultural and economic hub for all to enjoy. Thank you. Marisa Eng

subject: CIP Funding for the Liberty Park Greenhouse (Liberty Park Greenhouse - Envisioned / D5
comment: The Greenhouse at Liberty Park was built before 1922. It was beautiful! I remember being inside it many times over the years, and it was very depressing to see it fall into disrepair. Why do we do that in Salt Lake City? This building has an incredible amount of opportunity to educate our younger generations of students, right next to where they play. Make growing plants fun. I know it is a lot of fun for me. We are on the cusp of an ecological disaster where our planet is going to implode, and it will be too late. There is such an opportunity to teach the children of Salt Lake City about climate and how the right plants can make a huge difference. We should use the greenhouse to fill this void. Think of the educational classes you can have in the greenhouse, as well as outside in some or all of the open spaces that are around the greenhouse. Perhaps you show comparisons, building a normal Salt Lake garden of flowers, and track the water use to keep them alive. On the other side of the field, grow a garden that uses much less water, but looks just as pretty. Show the various waterwise grasses that will grow easily in Utah. This could be an educational piece of the Youth City program, teaching how to grow plants from seed, and then move them out into the open air and eventually harvest the tomatoes and other vegetables. It could be a wonderful field trip for elementary children around the valley. On Saturdays you could have demonstration classes outside that would include parents and children. There are so many educators here that could be the teachers, perhaps eventually teaching the Parks staff how to teach about plants and what makes them grow. It is also a great opportunity to teach people about trees and how they do need water even though they have been growing for 15 years without any water. Wait until the next windstorm, when the trees fall over because they aren't getting the water they need. Ask the Forestry Department and the Cemetery folks, what it takes to grow a tree. Show them a hollow, unwatered tree give the people of Utah the knowledge they need to keep the vegetation on earth alive, for their children. One class in second grade won't do it. It needs to be built into everyday life. Use the greenhouse and the space around it to start, and continue, that conversation. Fixing the greenhouse so it is usable is a small price to pay. Please approve the CIP funding for the restoration of this greenhouse. Judi Short

comment: Hello Dan, Late last summer or early fall by chance I met with Palmer DePaulis at an Allen Park special open house. They were holding a special event to let the public, especially their supporters, know about future for the complex. There were several options including different new buildings for several different proposed uses. Any and all of it seemed feasible. I haven't heard one thing about it since. In the meantime here at Crossroads we have been collaborating with one of our long time volunteers, Jeff White, on the possibility of providing manufactured housing for lower income residents of the city. I fact Jeff is under contract with the city housing authority to consult with them on various lower cost housing options. What Jeff has documented is that truly decent, affordable housing can be made available to lower income residents. So what? Several things. First, as I recall the Allen Park proposed plans offered the probability that some of the housing units would be made available to lower income individuals and maybe even families. I believe the intent is the units would house younger specialists with a particular interest in Allen Park, its history and environmental surrounding. Second, Jeff's special knowledge of the lower income housing and, especially, manufactured housing marks it as a feasible housing alternative in Allen Park. Palmer DePaulis sits on the city housing authority board and as a former mayor and public figure has shown a continuing concern for lower income residents. Palmer needs to know about manufactured housing and the city housing authority's interest. Third, Jeff, as a contractor cannot contact Palmer on his own. He feels it would be unprofessional for him to do so. I could try talking to Palmer but that might not get things going like it should. Help is needed. Upon a request from me representing Crossroads Urban Center would you be willing to listen to Jeff's manufactured housing proposal? If you find it promising would you contact Palmer and tell him as much. Then Palmer in turn can ask the housing authority staff what the situation might be. It could be the right thing for Allen Park and for some the other low income housing opportunities in the city. Plus you get a bird's eye view of the situation. Is this over reaching? No, not really. Manufactured housing is a real, ready to go option. The city housing authority can help deliver it in fast order. Like six months or so. Including Allen Park there are several building sites in on city owned property ready to go. Finally, just to be clear. I am doing this as a community advocate for the sake of the potential homeowners. Jeff is on a humble contract and just wants to get things moving. If it makes any difference to you we are also Judge Memorial graduates. Years apart we are but here to help out all the same. Thank you, Tim Funk Crossroads Urban Center

subject: Taxpayers don't want to subsidize stadium
comment: Dear City Councilmember: I urge you to oppose the proposed citywide sales tax increase that would give nearly $1 billion to the NHL sports/entertainment district. Inflation and growth have substantially increased the cost of housing, food, energy and other essential household expenses in recent years. These compounding costs amount to more than $11,000 a year for the average family of four! Many Salt Lake City residents simply cannot afford the additional estimated cost of $225 per year if this sales tax increase is approved. We should not be subsidizing businesses and billionaires at the expense of the average working family. The risks that private businesses choose to take should not be placed on the backs of taxpayers, especially when that business alone stands to reap the financial rewards! Study after study shows that these subsidies do not provide the promised economic benefits, and often leave taxpayers with broken promises and mounting costs in the long run. Please vote against this tax increase and subsidy! Sincerely, Tom Black

comment: Hi All, We now have about 180 completed surveys. Again, all are campers in SLC and all are struggling with a mental health or addiction problem. I was in Burger King on 400S 600W last night for about a half hour and counted what appeared to be 8 campers entering or leaving. I now understand I can just sit at any trax stop or corner in the downtown area and collect 20 surveys in about four hours. I can sit there reading a book, relaxing and get 20 surveys completed in no time. Easy. 6 days / 20 surveys will give us the 300 we need as a base for creating what could be a new narrative. The average arrests is 20. We have an extra chair if anyone would like to join us. Bernie

subject: Efficacy
comment: Hi All, The following was sent to a person interested in our effort to create an awareness of the current mental health "we can help you" systems level of effectiveness as it relates to homelessness and suicide. 3. I have been surveying the homeless campers in the area. 180 surveys. 80% of those I approached did the survey. 100% are dealing with a mental health or addiction problem. 100% have been in a "we can help you" program. A small follow up sample survey showed they had been arrested on average 20x and have been in at least 12 programs. That's 32 opportunities the current system had to help them and it failed. .....so all, is what we are doing actually helping people dealing with mental health and addictions issues? subject: SEG Project - Revitalization Tax
comment: Good Day All! You may have noted that many Salt Lake residents have expressed concern over the Rev Tax on citizens, especially that the tax will not be shared outright with surrounding communities. For me, as a community leader with the North West Community Council, the concern is particularly applicable as our west side communities are populated by lower income statuses than other parts of the city. Considerations to share revenue in your deliberations: 1. Lower the tax rate; 2. appropriate 10% of the current tax rate with residents, forming an advisory committee noting how such a share will be spent perhaps in the form of Item 3; and, 3. Create an interlocal agreement such as exists with the Utah Inland Port Authority whereby revenue is shared with the community: "The Parties desire to enter into this Agreement to comply with Utah law, to establish a contractual relationship creating certainty on the 25-year distribution of the City Differential to UIPA and to commit to a process for the expenditure of a portion of the City Differential". For many, the tax issue condenses to fairness: A) city residents paying for a statewide public benefit, B) the burden on financially vulnerable communities, C) increased traffic/infrastructure burden on the city from statewide and national attendees, and, D) communities have had limited time to review the recently released contract. For example, before reaching a decision, hold public meetings to gain input; some may be negative but others may offer insights on how to improve the tax issue. Public outreach will also improve public trust. Best, Terry Marasco

subject: traffic calming on Ken Rey St
comment: Dear Jon and Dan, First of all, thank you for your consistent efforts to improve pedestrian safety in Salt Lake City. It is comforting to know that we share the vision of a city where pedestrians and cyclists have an equal right to safe passage on streets as motorists. Re-training drivers to be courteous and careful is a tall order and the Bonneville Road Safety Committee appreciates your support and funding for traffic calming. The measures being implemented are saving lives. A member of our committee, Eddie Karasik, brought to our attention this week that the City was able to install traffic calming white pylons where Kensington Ave, Bryan Ave, and Ken Rey St merge. Given the width of Ken Rey and the lack of signage approaching this intersection, speeding and disorder have been the norm. If three roads meet and no drivers are instructed to yield, at some point a bad accident is bound to occur where two drivers assume they have the right of way or try to beat the other car through the intersection. Eddie mentioned that the white pylons seem to be doing a good job of slowing drivers and directing them around the middle of the intersection rather than right through it. However, some neighbors do not like how the white pylons look and it sounds like they have been voicing their concerns. I wonder if the City and this neighborhood could come together and meet both safety needs and aesthetic preferences by installing a small roundabout in this intersection. I happen to live just below where Princeton Ave, Herbert Ave, and Yale Ave meet and the small (greenery-filled) roundabout is attractive and helps all cars navigate this intersection safely. I have attached both a picture of the roundabout as well as a map. Please let me know how we, as a committee and concerned neighborhood citizens, can support the City's efforts to fulfill the Livable Streets Program's traffic calming improvements on Ken Rey St. Looking forward to hearing your thoughts, Lauren

subject: My thoughts on the sports complex
comment: Dan, I'm not sure what happened and why you voted in favor of this. I think you owe it to D6 to be transparent about these things before voting and the lack of transparency is really troubling. Here's the reality, from the mouths of experts: "These are luxury palaces that are being built that are exclusive and limited to some of the wealthiest people in the city," Bradbury said. "So why is the government subsidizing this? These could easily be privately funded and we know that because that's how baseball came into existence." "There's no evidence that stadiums are economic development catalysts and, in fact, they tend to have some very big detriments," he said, noting that they bring crime and their sporadic use can discourage stable businesses like grocery stores. "They're just very bad anchors for economic development," Bradbury said. "This bill is a lose-lose for Utah taxpayers, who will face higher taxes and fewer public services as a result," said AFP-Utah executive director Kevin Greene. "While every Utahn would be excited for new sports teams, the wealthy sports franchises who want new stadiums should foot the bill themselves. If a billion dollars of hardworking families' money is the price to play ball, Utah shouldn't play the game at all." It's clear that SLC residents should not be footing the bill. We deserve an explanation for why you voted how you did. Brad. On Tue, Jul 9, 2024 at 6:58 PM Brad Bush <bfbush@gmail.com> wrote: Dan, Just reiterating my opposition to the use of taxpayer funds to support the SEG stadium work. This entire initiative is very focused on glossy pictures and light on details and a project with all the telltale signs of a major money loser for residents to the benefit of a multi-billionaire. The only fathomable rationale for this would be that the city could guarantee higher benefit than cost to each resident. Otherwise, this just becomes a wealth transfer tax hike. But all the economic analysis on this topic points to these kinds of boondoggles as money losers for residents. The primary driver for people like Mendenhall is to burnish image, which is a benefit pocketed in real time, while the community pays costs over decades. Key institutions like Abravanel Hall shouldn't be impacted. Ultimately, Smith has few options besides SLC and he loses going south. If there's a path for the city to benefit without financial contribution, tax hikes or negative impact to existing institutions, great. But none of us should be footing the bill or paying the price for this. SLC would be better off passing on this than having this project blight the downtown and putting residents on the hook for the bill. And I'll also be candid that the lack of communication from your side on walking on this issue and the details on what's on the table needs to be better. A D6 newsletter would do a lot to keep residents updated. Brad

Your efforts do not go unnoticed, and I am grateful for your commitment to making Salt Lake City a better place for all of us. Now, let's talk trash—literally. I am writing to urge you to consider implementing a ban on single-use plastic bags in Salt Lake City. I know, I know, we've all heard the same song and dance about how banning these pesky plastic nuisances might hurt businesses, but bear with me. I believe there's a sensible, phased approach that can work for everyone. Phase 1: Education and Incentives Let's start by rolling out a citywide campaign to educate residents and businesses about the environmental impact of single-use plastics. Offer incentives for businesses to switch to more sustainable alternatives, like compostable bags or encouraging customers to bring their own reusable bags. Maybe a little friendly competition between neighborhoods with prizes for the most reduced plastic use? Who doesn't love a good contest? Phase 2: Partial Ban After a year of education and incentives, we could introduce a partial ban. Focus on the major culprits first—grocery stores, big-box retailers, and chain stores. Give them a six-month grace period to transition, and provide support for small businesses to help them make the switch. Phase 3: Full Ban Once the community has adjusted to the changes, we can implement a full ban on single-use plastic bags citywide. This phased approach will allow businesses and residents to adapt gradually, mitigating any potential negative impacts. Believe it or not, some surprising places have already seen great success with similar bans. Rwanda, yes, Rwanda, has had a nationwide ban on plastic bags since 2008, and it's cleaner than ever. Closer to home, cities like San Francisco and Austin have seen significant reductions in plastic waste since implementing their bans. Even Laredo, Texas—a place you might not expect to be a green pioneer—banned single-use plastic bags back in 2015. Unfortunately the Texas courts overruled the Austin and Laredo bans but they are still cases of note. My understanding is that this should not be a problem in Utah as PC has some version of a bag ban. Beyond the environmental impact, I view the single-use plastics issue as an equity issue. All of the city's rainwater flows down to the Jordan River, which runs through District 2. As a result, we disproportionately have to deal with everyone else's litteral garbage. I spend at least one morning a week pulling plastic bags and trash out of my parkstrip because of the sheer amount of litter. It's not just unsightly; it's unfair. Our community deserves better. I know the idea of a plastic bag ban might seem daunting, but think of the upsides. Fewer plastic bags fluttering in the breeze like ghostly jellyfish, less trash clogging our waterways, and a cleaner, more beautiful city for everyone. Plus, it might save me from becoming the neighborhood's unofficial trash collector! Thank you for considering this proposal. I genuinely appreciate your hard work and dedication to our community, and I believe that together, we can make Salt Lake City a leader in sustainability and equity. Warm regards, Erik P.S. If you need help getting plastic bags out of the parkstrip, you know where to find me. I'm getting pretty good at it!

Third, number of hours someone works for doesn't always equal how well the job gets done. So why should an unskilled or distracted worker get paid more based on how many hours it has taken? (I'm not implying any of you being an unskilled worker.) Fourth, by giving yourselves another raise*, you will be taking funds away from something else. Are those funds something you didn't need in the first place? Less amount was adequate? subject: Support for Rio Grande Plan
comment: Dear Councilman Dugan, I am writing to ask that you support Salt Lake City's Rio Grande Proposal. This proposal would greatly improve our state by removing several dangerous railroad crossings (including 200S, 800S and 900S to name a few) and opening over 70 acres for development. This project would improve the experience of commuters and long-distance travelers, all while helping to begin the healing of the east-west divide in Salt Lake City. A new central station located at the Rio Grande Depot would be a strong welcome to those who travel to Utah via train. It would provide significantly more amenities than the existing Salt Lake Central Station, all while being closer to downtown. The Rio Grande Plan proposes the relocation of the tracks into a "Train Box" along 500 West. This Train Box would be a shallow tunnel wide enough for up to six train tracks allowing for all connections to the current system to be maintained and expanded. Our city prepared for the 2002 Olympics by cutting back the freeway viaducts to where they are today, the Rio Grande Plan would allow these ramps to be shortened once more, opening up valuable street frontage. The estimated price tag of this project is similar to UDOT's I-15 widening between Farmington and Salt Lake City, making the Rio Grande Plan an ideal project to complete before the Olympics. If this project were pursued as an Olympic transportation infrastructure project it would likely receive significant federal funding to reduce the burden on Utah's taxpayers. The transportation legacy of the 2002 Winter Olympics are the billions of dollars of freeway projects completed leading up to the games. Most of the 2002 Olympic freeway improvements are still serving Utah well, allowing for transit projects such as The Rio Grande Proposal to be a focus in 2034. As the state continues to expand, we need to be looking for more sustainable development. I believe the Rio Grande Plan would help us build a more sustainable Utah. Expanding the freeways would result in increased traffic and pollution from the volume of cars on the road, a rising heat index from the concrete and asphalt structures absorbing heat, and decreased walkability, access to public transit, and dependence on cars in an already congested state. It's been proven repeatedly that expanding freeways doesn't alleviate traffic, and I don't feel that Utah should be putting valuable time and resources into something that wouldn't benefit the residents. Please show your support for the Rio Grande plan, which would continue to benefit Utah for generations to come. Thanks, Marisa Lee Salt Lake City, UT

subject: Rio Grande Plan
comment: Dear Members of the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to express my strong support for the Rio Grande Plan and to encourage you to choose this visionary project as a critical step in the ongoing revitalization of our city. The Rio Grande neighborhood holds a significant place in Salt Lake City's history, and it is essential that we invest in its future by addressing the challenges it currently faces. The comprehensive approach outlined in the Rio Grande Plan, with its focus on homelessness, public safety, urban redevelopment, and community engagement, reflects the values and priorities of our city. By adopting this plan, we have the opportunity to transform the Rio Grande area into a vibrant, safe, and inclusive neighborhood that honors its historical significance while meeting the needs of today's residents and businesses. Addressing homelessness in our community is of paramount importance. The plan's commitment to relocating and improving homeless services, along with the provision of permanent supportive housing, offers a compassionate and effective solution. By providing individuals experiencing homelessness with the resources they need to regain stability, we can create a more equitable and humane city. Moreover, enhancing public safety in the Rio Grande area is crucial for fostering a sense of security and well-being among all who live, work, and visit the neighborhood. The plan's strategies for increasing law enforcement presence and improving public safety measures will help reduce crime and create a welcoming environment for everyone. The proposed urban redevelopment initiatives, which include restoring historic buildings and promoting mixed-use developments, will breathe new life into the Rio Grande neighborhood. These efforts will not only preserve the area's cultural heritage but also attract new businesses and residents, contributing to the overall economic vitality of Salt Lake City. Lastly, I commend the emphasis on community engagement in the Rio Grande Plan. Ensuring that the voices of local residents, businesses, and organizations are heard and considered is essential for the success of any redevelopment effort. I am confident that, with continued collaboration and dialogue, the Rio Grande Plan will reflect the diverse needs and aspirations of our community. In conclusion, I urge you to endorse the Rio Grande Plan and take the necessary steps to implement this comprehensive and forward-thinking project. By doing so, we can create a brighter future for the Rio Grande neighborhood and for Salt Lake City as a whole. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Kaitlyn Gatchel Herriman

subject: Support for CIP Public Infrastructure Improvements on Fayette Avenue
comment: Dear Dan Dugan, The Central Ninth Community Council is requesting your support for the CIP public infrastructure improvements project on Fayette Avenue. This initiative, spanning from Washington Street to 200 West, represents a significant step forward in enhancing the quality of life for our community. The proposed project is poised to address several key aspects that are crucial for fostering a vibrant, walkable, and safe neighborhood. By completing street and parking paving on the south side of Fayette Avenue, installing a sidewalk, curb, and gutter on the north side, and lighting on both sides, the project will significantly enhance pedestrian accessibility and safety. The planned enhancements—including the paving of a parking area, installation of street trees, landscaping, and street lighting—will not only beautify the area but also contribute to the overall functionality and appeal of the neighborhood. This project is especially noteworthy in light of its proximity to the 900 South TRAX stop, which underscores the importance of walkability in supporting public transit usage and reducing reliance on personal vehicles. The integration of these improvements aligns with the zoning goals for the area (FBUN-2) and the broader vision of creating a walkable community. This project will be a significant asset to our community, addressing critical issues related to walkability, open space, and parking. The synergy between the proposed city-funded improvements and UDOT and UTA initiatives will foster a more cohesive and inviting environment for residents and visitors alike. I strongly urge the City Council to support and approve the funding for this project. Your support will be instrumental in realizing these much-needed improvements and in contributing to the ongoing revitalization of our community. Thank you for your attention to this important matter. Should you require any additional information or wish to discuss this project further, please do not hesitate to contact me. Sincerely, Douglas Flagler Central Ninth Community Council Chair

subject: Memory Grove & City Creek Parks Improvement Grant
comment: Dear Members of the Salt Lake City Council, On behalf of Preservation Utah, I am writing to express our strong support for the proposed improvements to Memory Grove and City Creek Parks, as included in the Mayor's 2025 budget. For the past 30 years, we have had the privilege of operating Memorial House within Memory Grove Park, and we have witnessed firsthand the importance of these parks as historical and cultural landmarks in our community. Memory Grove and City Creek Parks are beautiful green spaces that serve as living memorials to our community's history. They are places where citizens and visitors alike can reflect on the past while enjoying Salt Lake City's natural beauty. However, the passage of time has led to significant wear and tear on the parks' infrastructure, and many of the monuments and pathways now need urgent repair. The proposed improvements are essential for preserving the integrity and safety of these beloved parks. Replacing the deteriorating street lamp poles, refurbishing the historic monuments, and enhancing pedestrian safety on the switchbacks are crucial to ensure they remain safe, welcoming, and historically accurate for all who visit. We also strongly support the development of a Preservation & Maintenance Plan for Memory Grove Park and the Freedom Trail. This plan will provide a roadmap for the long-term care of these parks, ensuring that they continue to serve as vital parts of our community. Thank you for considering this important matter. Sincerely, Brandy Strand Executive Director preservationutah.org

Bruce Markosian Date: August 5, 2024 at 3:18:08 PM MDT To: alejandro.puy@slcgov.com Subject: Water/Sewer Stabilization Fees - Acct #W1046469 Hello: I want you to be aware of a grossly unfair billing resulting from the recent water/sewer stabilization fees. My family owns an industrial property at REDACTED that, since the death of my father in 1998, I have managed. The property is served by three water meters and, for the entire time I have been in charge, one of those meters has never been used. It is a mystery as to why that meter was ever installed but, regardless of it's essential uselessness, I have paid the monthly service fee stated I was told by the water department I would have to completely remove the meter/water line to eliminate the billing. Now, with the stabilization fees the latest monthly charge is $864, more than a tenfold jump!! This is outrageous!! I can not imagine this was ever your intent when you approved the fees and I request immediate action and a billing adjustment to correct this oversight. Sincerely, Bruce Markosian, GP AAM Investments Ltd.

subject: CIP Budget Comments: #451562: Pedestrian Safety / HAWK at Richmond St. and Zenith Ave.
comment: Dear City Council Members, I've been a District 7 resident for 3 years, living at REDACTED with my family. I'm sharing budget comments about CIP application #451562: Pedestrian Safety / HAWK at Richmond St. and Zenith Ave. The Richmond/Zenith intersection is in the growing Brickyard area and is part of the 1300 E Reconstruction Project. My neighbors and I walk kids to daycare, use the 213 bus stops, and travel to Nibley Park School through the Zenith/Richmond intersection. Although there is considerable pedestrian traffic that will only continue to grow, this 5-lane intersection remains inadequately equipped to protect those walking, biking, and using transit. I've been involved in, and have witnessed, countless near-misses with cars hitting pedestrians. Just this morning, cars were trying to pass other cars that stopped while my husband and toddler were walking in the crosswalk. Drivers speed between the controlled intersections at Highland and Brickyard, and do not see or ignore the flashing yellow lights and pedestrians at the Richmond/Zenith crosswalk. Neighbors who signed the CIP petition described this intersection as "scary," a "nightmare," and "dangerous." Although there are benefits to including a HAWK installation as part of the 1300 E project, my understanding is this CIP application has so far been denied due to its estimated cost of $500,000. I've heard from our councilperson that this cost could be split: $50,000 to design the project this year and then $450,000 for construction next year. My family and I support this compromise with the addition of lower-cost, interim pedestrian protections. Crosswalk paint, pedestrian flags, and state law signs in the crosswalk are some ideas for lower-cost safety improvements to this intersection. Anything the city can install while we wait for a HAWK signal will improve pedestrian safety. Thank you for your time and I hope to receive your support for funding $50,000 to design this project and install lower-cost pedestrian safety measures this coming year. Sincerely, Laura Kendellen

subject: Sports Entertainment District Agreement Needs Additional Stipulations for a better Sports Entertainment District
comment: Dear Sen. McCay, Sen. Cullimore, Rep. Moss, Rep. Hawkins, and Mr. Pierpont, I'm writing to ask that you get a better deal for Utah's taxpayers and for Salt Lake City with the Sports entertainment district. The general idea of the Sports and Entertainment District could be great for SLC. I think keeping the Jazz and the Utah Hockey Club sound great. However, we know from many studies that cities don't often get a true benefit from this. So, let's make this better. It's a contract after all and SEG doesn't seem to have too many obligations here. I do not understand why you cannot stipulate more from SEG in the contract. They are getting $900M of our money yet they seem to have few obligations other than the current zoning in place. The following provisions need to be added to the contract: 1. Better metrics on free tickets to low income people. Not just 'various games' but all games. 2. Include a non-car transportation plan/Travel Demand Management program. The traffic study that was included is for cars only and is really unacceptably bad. There's no mention of TRAX, Bus, FrontRunner, Walking, Biking, or reducing parking (which thus incentivizes more sustainable transportation). Non-car transportation needs to be spelled out in the contract. SLC has a commitment to sustainability- this contract does not hold true to that. 3. NBA and NHL provisions are spelled out. What if we get a WNBA team, women's hockey, arena football, or other big time sport? There needs to be contingencies for this too. 4. Some sort of plan for the Salt Palace. Just giving SEG control of this seems like a bad plan. Stipulations are needed. 5. The low-income housing surcharge is great, but not tied to inflation or anything. Now it sounds like a good bit of money, but in 20 years? Not so much. Please tie this to inflation and cost of living index. 6. There's little in the agreement that I see about ensuring public access and right of way to spaces that are currently public. SLC made this mistake when they sold a block of Main Street years ago and this space is not 24/7 public space. Please don't repeat this mistake. Current public spaces need to be kept public 24/7. 7. There is no sustainability requirement. They really need to agree to higher building standards and alternative energy use (solar etc) as part of the construction process. SLC has had a commitment to sustainability- this contract does not hold true to that. 8. With the Olympics coming in 2034, it should be part of the contract that SLC can use the facilities for the Olympics at no cost for renting the facilities. 9. The plans show nothing about a bike path or bike lanes on 300 W to N. Temple. There's some vague mention of this, but no requirement. This needs to be part of the contract. 10. There's little mention of bike facilities on any of the other roads leading to the Entertainment District. Please include those. 11. The contract has nothing about requiring bike parking on the facilities. There is currently no bike parking at the Delta Center. Since the renovations would be just that, there would be no zoning requirement to add bike parking since it's not a new construction project. Please include this so that people can more easily get to the Arena in a sustainable fashion. 12. A requirement for a percentage of locally owned businesses in the Entertainment District. 13. No destruction of Abrvenal Hall. This should be a stipulation. Yes, I'm aware that this is an SLCo facility. 14. No heliport - this should be a stipulation. While there are no plans for one, this should be permanently off the table. 15. Not a strong enough contract that would prevent the teams from leaving. 16. There is only the possibility of 2 SLC run public events from May 1 to September 15. This is problematic since it's only about 1/3 of the year and thus misses out on events during other times that the city might want to promote. And, it does not include February which is when the Olympics would be here. Why not have this be one per month for the entire year? These are just a few of the omissions that I found in a first reading of the contract. I'm sure that there are more, but these are glaring omissions and need to be corrected. We all want SLC to be vibrant, sustainable, and open. Please ensure this by updating the agreement. Thank you, Dave Iltis Salt Lake City resident Cycling Utah

subject: Please expand SLC trails per the Master Plan!
comment: I would like to write in support of the expansion of the Foothill trail system and the implementation of the master plan. As a citizen who has lived in the Avenues from 2006 until recently, the expansion of our trail system has been exciting and long overdue! The new trails are fantastic, and I have been enjoying them immensely with my kids. Salt Lake has world-class recreation, but it hasn't had a world-class trail system to match. Now it can! I am concerned that a small vociferous minority may be successful in continuing to halt further trail development. I can personally attest that these trails are more popular than ever, and the new trails are a big reason for this. Sadly, the old trail system is not sustainable. Many trails went straight up hills and became terribly eroded over the years. In addition, (mostly) hikers made more and more unofficial, unsustainable "wildcat" trails that have multiplied as our population has grown. Having new separate biking and hiking trails has also diminished confrontations as well. And I feel that the main threat to our foothills is not a new network of trails—it's climate change. We need to keep our recreation local. People move to SLC for our world-class recreation. If we don't have a commensurate world-class trail network, people will continue to go elsewhere—the Cottonwoods, Draper, Park City—to seek out trails and emit tons of carbon dioxide as they drive to do so. As a SLC high-school mountain bike coach, I feel that we have to travel much further than need be to access suitable trails. It has been more discouraging to see trails continuing to expand in the foothills of North Salt Lake, Bountiful, Millcreek, and Draper but not in Salt Lake proper. Please continue the great work you all are doing and continue to expand our trails. I hope that you do not let a vocal minority dissuade you from doing so.

subject: Please continue with the Foothills Trail System Master Plan!
comment: I am an Avenues resident that regularly uses the trails that have been completed to date under the Foothills Trail System Master Plan. They are a huge asset and have held up incredibly well over the past few years - in other words the concerns expressed about the "construction methods" of these trails appear to be completely unfounded. The full Foothills Trail System Master Plan has been held up for 3+ years by a vocal, anti-progress minority of Avenues residents. It is frankly disappointing that the Council bought into idea that we needed to "Save Our Foothills" when exactly what they needed saving from was never clear to me (and many of my neighbors). To me, the resistance to the Plan was NIMBYism, plain and simple. As time has gone, not having a comprehensive plan has done more harm than good as users continue to use social trails, including some mostly completed trails in the Plan (at the top of Dry Creek for example). It is time to move forward with the Foothills Trail System Master Plan and continue building a world class trail system right in the heart of our city!

subject: In Support of Trail Development
comment: Please accept this message in support of trail development in the Foothills. One of the key components of the master plan, that I believe is integral to accessibility and usability of the Foothills Trail System is the development of trails and specifically, the development of use-specific trails. While I understand that there are concerns about building downhill bike trails, and how that impacts hiking users of the trail system, I believe strongly that the development of downhill only trails is integral to the future development of this area. As is the case at many nearby recreation areas (Corner Canyon and Park City, for example) having downhill only bike trails increases the safety and accessibility of all users. The foothills area is used extensively by both cyclists and hikers. While hikers may be uncomfortable with being told they cannot use a downhill mountain biking trail, to neglect the benefits of downhill only trails is to neglect that cyclists regularly use this area. Since cycling has been, and will continue to be, a significant use of this area, I believe that the best way forward is to acknowledge that and plan accordingly. Furthermore, the population of Salt Lake City is growing quickly, with one of the large appeals to many moving to the area is the accessibility of outdoor pursuits to the city. Expanding the trail system will increase this access and provide greater good to a greater number of users. I understand the concerns from residents of the area that the trails they know are changing, however I am concerned that these objections are made by a small group of people whose concerns are narrow in scope, failing to understand the value of public lands to the more general public. While demands for more thorough environmental impact assessments may appear to be well-meaning, I believe this is a tactic may simply be used to delay the project or reduce its feasibility.
